claim: Cell layers eliminate unwanted cells through the extrusion process, which underlines healthy versus flawed tissue behaviors.
source: Cell layers eliminate unwanted cells through the extrusion process, which underlines healthy versus flawed tissue behaviors.
evidence: This is a general statement about cell extrusion that draws from established scientific understanding of tissue biology.

claim: The underlying mechanical basis including the forces involved in cellular extrusion remains largely unexplored.
source: Although several biochemical pathways have been identified, the underlying mechanical basis including the forces involved in cellular extrusion remains largely unexplored.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, based on inference from existing literature.

claim: By increasing relative cell–cell adhesion forces the cell monolayer can switch between the collective tendency towards fivefold, hexatic, disclinations relative to half-integer, nematic, defects for extruding a cell.
source: Specifically, we show that by increasing relative cell–cell adhesion forces the cell monolayer can switch between the collective tendency towards fivefold, hexatic, disclinations relative to half-integer, nematic, defects for extruding a cell.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data presented in the manuscript showing the relationship between adhesion forces and extrusion mechanisms.

claim: An extrusion event acts as a mechanism to relieve localized stress concentration.
source: We unify our findings by accessing three-dimensional mechanical stress fields to show that an extrusion event acts as a mechanism to relieve localized stress concentration.
evidence: This is supported by stress field analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cells actively coordinate their movements through mechanosensitive adhesion complexes at the cell–substrate interface and cell–cell junctions.
source: Advanced experimental techniques have linked this ability to mechanical interactions between cells (Maskarinec et al., 2009; Ladoux, 2009; Ladoux and Mège, 2017). Specifically, cells actively coordinate their movements through mechanosensitive adhesion complexes at the cell–substrate interface and cell–cell junctions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Cell–cell and cell–substrate adhesions seem to be coupled.
source: Moreover, cell–cell and cell–substrate adhesions seem to be coupled (Balasubramaniam et al., 2021), further complicating the interplay of mechanics with biochemistry.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: A majority of current approaches to simulate multicellular layers are limited to two-dimensional systems.
source: While advances in experimental techniques are followed by more nuanced theoretical and computational developments, a majority of current approaches to simulate multicellular layers are limited to two-dimensional systems, hindering in-depth exploration of intrinsically three-dimensional nature of the distinct forces that govern cell–cell and cell–substrate interactions.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of computational modeling in the field.

claim: Cell extrusion is inherently three-dimensional.
source: Furthermore, some of the most fundamental processes in cell biology such as cell extrusion – responsible for tissue integrity – are inherently three-dimensional.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of the nature of cell extrusion.

claim: Cell extrusion refers to the process of removal of excess cells to prevent accumulation of unnecessary or pathological cells.
source: Cell extrusion refers to the process of removal of excess cells to prevent accumulation of unnecessary or pathological cells (Rosenblatt et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Cell extrusion can get initiated through apoptotic signaling.
source: This process can get initiated through apoptotic signaling (Rosenblatt et al., 2001), oncogenic transformation (Hogan et al., 2009), and overcrowding of cells (Marinari et al., 2012; Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Levayer et al., 2016) or induced by replication stress (Dwivedi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Cell extrusion can get initiated through oncogenic transformation.
source: This process can get initiated through apoptotic signaling (Rosenblatt et al., 2001), oncogenic transformation (Hogan et al., 2009), and overcrowding of cells (Marinari et al., 2012; Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Levayer et al., 2016) or induced by replication stress (Dwivedi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Cell extrusion can get initiated through overcrowding of cells.
source: This process can get initiated through apoptotic signaling (Rosenblatt et al., 2001), oncogenic transformation (Hogan et al., 2009), and overcrowding of cells (Marinari et al., 2012; Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Levayer et al., 2016) or induced by replication stress (Dwivedi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Cell extrusion can be induced by replication stress.
source: This process can get initiated through apoptotic signaling (Rosenblatt et al., 2001), oncogenic transformation (Hogan et al., 2009), and overcrowding of cells (Marinari et al., 2012; Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Levayer et al., 2016) or induced by replication stress (Dwivedi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Cell extrusion plays an important role in developmental processes.
source: Most importantly, cell extrusion plays an important role in developmental (Toyama et al., 2008), homeostatic (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Le et al., 2021), and pathological processes (Slattum and Rosenblatt, 2014), including cancer metastasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cell extrusion plays an important role in homeostatic processes.
source: Most importantly, cell extrusion plays an important role in developmental (Toyama et al., 2008), homeostatic (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Le et al., 2021), and pathological processes (Slattum and Rosenblatt, 2014), including cancer metastasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cell extrusion plays an important role in pathological processes including cancer metastasis.
source: Most importantly, cell extrusion plays an important role in developmental (Toyama et al., 2008), homeostatic (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; Le et al., 2021), and pathological processes (Slattum and Rosenblatt, 2014), including cancer metastasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The underlying mechanisms that facilitate cell extrusion are still unclear.
source: However, the underlying mechanisms that facilitate cell extrusion are still unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Cellular systems feature nematic order.
source: The similarities between cellular systems and liquid crystals, studied both theoretically and experimentally, featuring both nematic order (Saw et al., 2017; Kawaguchi et al., 2017; Duclos et al., 2018; Blanch-Mercader et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021) and hexatic order (Classen et al., 2005; Sugimura and Ishihara, 2013; Pasupalak et al., 2020; Maitra et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022) with the two phases potentially coexisting (Armengol-Collado et al., 2022) and interacting provide a fresh perspective for understanding cellular processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Cellular systems feature hexatic order.
source: The similarities between cellular systems and liquid crystals, studied both theoretically and experimentally, featuring both nematic order (Saw et al., 2017; Kawaguchi et al., 2017; Duclos et al., 2018; Blanch-Mercader et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021) and hexatic order (Classen et al., 2005; Sugimura and Ishihara, 2013; Pasupalak et al., 2020; Maitra et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022) with the two phases potentially coexisting (Armengol-Collado et al., 2022) and interacting provide a fresh perspective for understanding cellular processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Nematic and hexatic phases can potentially coexist in cellular systems.
source: The similarities between cellular systems and liquid crystals, studied both theoretically and experimentally, featuring both nematic order (Saw et al., 2017; Kawaguchi et al., 2017; Duclos et al., 2018; Blanch-Mercader et al., 2018; Tan et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021) and hexatic order (Classen et al., 2005; Sugimura and Ishihara, 2013; Pasupalak et al., 2020; Maitra et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022) with the two phases potentially coexisting (Armengol-Collado et al., 2022) and interacting provide a fresh perspective for understanding cellular processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Fivefold disclinations in hexatic arrangement of cells favor overlaps between the cells in two-dimensions.
source: The fivefold disclinations in hexatic arrangement of cells are numerically shown to favor overlaps between the cells in two-dimensions (Loewe et al., 2020), potentially contributing to the cell extrusion in three-dimensions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous numerical work.

claim: A net positive charge associated with hexatic disclinations can be associated with the maximum curvature of dome-like structures in model organoids and in epithelial cell layers.
source: In this vein, it is shown that a net positive charge associated with hexatic disclinations can be associated with the maximum curvature of dome-like structures in model organoids and in epithelial cell layers (Rozman et al., 2020; Rozman et al., 2021; Hoffmann et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In cellular monolayers, comet- and trefoil-shaped half-integer topological defects, corresponding to +1/2 and -1/2 charges, respectively, are prevalent.
source: Moreover, in cellular monolayers, comet- and trefoil-shaped half-integer topological defects, corresponding to +1/2 and -1/2 charges, respectively, are prevalent (Doostmohammadi et al., 2015; Doostmohammadi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Half-integer topological defects are singular points in cellular alignment that mark the breakdown of orientational order.
source: These are singular points in cellular alignment that mark the breakdown of orientational order (de Genne and Prost, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on liquid crystals.

claim: Recent experiments on epithelial monolayers found a strong correlation between extrusion events and the position of a subset of +1/2 defects.
source: Recent experiments on epithelial monolayers found a strong correlation between extrusion events and the position of a subset of +1/2 defects in addition to a relatively weaker correlation with -1/2 defects (Saw et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Recent experiments on epithelial monolayers found a relatively weaker correlation between extrusion events and -1/2 defects.
source: Recent experiments on epithelial monolayers found a strong correlation between extrusion events and the position of a subset of +1/2 defects in addition to a relatively weaker correlation with -1/2 defects (Saw et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: The purely biological consensus is that an extruding cell sends a signal to its neighbor that activates its elimination process.
source: These recently introduced purely mechanical routes to cell extrusion have opened the door to new questions on the nature of forces that are involved in eliminating cells from the monolayer and challenge the purely biological consensus that an extruding cell sends a signal to its neighbor that activates its elimination process (Rosenblatt et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In the absence of self-propulsion forces, the initial configuration tends to equilibrate into a hexagonal lattice.
source: In the absence of self-propulsion forces, the initial configuration tends to equilibrate into a hexagonal lattice (see Appendix 1—figure 11 in Appendix 1 for an example).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in the appendix.

claim: As self-propulsion forces associated with front-rear cell polarity are introduced, the system is pushed away from its equilibrium hexagonal configuration, resulting in defects manifested as fivefold and sevenfold disclinations.
source: As we introduce self-propulsion forces associated with front-rear cell polarity (see 'Materials and methods' for polarization dynamics), the system is pushed away from its equilibrium hexagonal configuration, resulting in defects manifested as fivefold and sevenfold disclinations, as shown in Figure 2b.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The simulations show the continuous emergence of half-integer (±1/2), nematic, topological defects that spontaneously nucleate in pairs and follow chaotic trajectories before annihilation.
source: The results (example snapshot in Figure 2a) show the continuous emergence of half-integer (±1/2), nematic, topological defects that spontaneously nucleate in pairs and follow chaotic trajectories before annihilation (see Appendix 1—figure 9 in Appendix 1 for energy spectra characterization).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2a and Appendix 1—figure 9.

claim: The nematic defects emerge in the absence of any active dipolar stress or subcellular fields as the only active driving in these simulations is the polar force that the cells generate.
source: It is noteworthy that unlike previous studies of active nematic behavior in 2D cell layers (Mueller et al., 2019; Wenzel and Voigt, 2021), the nematic defects here emerge in the absence of any active dipolar stress or subcellular fields as the only active driving in these simulations is the polar force that the cells generate.
evidence: This is a statement about the simulation setup and its distinction from previous work.

claim: Although the cells are endowed with polarity in terms of their self-propulsion, the emergent symmetry in terms of their orientational alignment is nematic.
source: Therefore, although the cells are endowed with polarity in terms of their self-propulsion, the emergent symmetry in terms of their orientational alignment is nematic, which is in line with experimental observations in cell monolayers (Saw et al., 2017; Blanch-Mercader et al., 2018), discrete models of self-propelled rods (Bär et al., 2020; Meacock et al., 2021), and recently proposed continuum model of polar active matter (Amiri et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data and citations to previous experimental and theoretical work.

claim: Extrusion events can be correlated with the position of both +1/2 comet-shaped and -1/2 trefoil-shaped topological defects.
source: Remarkably, in accordance with experimental observations (Saw et al., 2017), we find that the extrusion events can be correlated with the position of both +1/2 comet-shaped and -1/2 trefoil-shaped topological defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data and citation to previous experimental work.

claim: Laser ablation experiments have established that an induced extrusion event does not favor the nucleation of a pair of nematic defects.
source: Furthermore, laser ablation experiments have established that an induced extrusion event does not favor the nucleation of a pair of nematic defects (Saw et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: A Kolmogorov–Smirnov test rejects the hypothesis that simulation-based extrusion events are uncorrelated with the half-integer nematic defects.
source: The results of the KS test reject this (see Appendix 1—table 1 and Appendix 1—figure 1 in Appendix 1) and thus falsify the hypothesis that simulation-based extrusion events are uncorrelated with the half-integer nematic defects.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of simulation data.

claim: The coordination number is independent of apical or basal considerations.
source: The coordination number is determined based on the interactions of cells (see Appendix 1) and this property is independent of apical or basal considerations (Kaliman et al., 2021), unlike geometrical structures called scutoids that have been identified in curved epithelial tubes (Gómez-Gálvez et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Increasing cell–substrate adhesion leads to lower extrusion events.
source: In our simulations, increasing cell–substrate adhesion leads to lower extrusion events (see Appendix 1—figure 8 in Appendix 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Appendix 1—figure 8.

claim: Other studies with confluent cellular layers have also found Lewis's relations to not be valid.
source: While in our simulations the cell monolayers are not always confluent due to the extrusion events, other studies with confluent cellular layers have also found such relations to not be valid (Kim et al., 2014; Wenzel et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The projected area of an extruding cell decreases prior to extrusion, but the number of interacting neighbors generally does not change in that time frame.
source: In our simulations, the projected area of an extruding cell decreases prior to extrusion, but the number of interacting neighbors generally does not change in that time frame (see Appendix 1—figure 4 in Appendix 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: Cell extrusion emerges as a consequence of cells pushing and pulling on their neighbors due to their intrinsic activity.
source: Together, these results suggest mechanical rather than geometrical routes to cell extrusion. Specifically, in our approach cell extrusion emerges as a consequence of cells pushing and pulling on their neighbors due to their intrinsic activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the simulation results presented.

claim: The approach contrasts with inherently threshold-based vertex models for both cellular rearrangements (T1 transitions) and extrusions (T2 transitions).
source: This contrasts with inherently threshold-based vertex models (see, e.g., Okuda and Fujimoto, 2020) for both cellular rearrangements (T1 transitions) and extrusions (T2 transitions).
evidence: This is a comparison with previous modeling approaches supported by citation.

claim: The occurrence of disclinations in a flat surface produces local stress concentration.
source: The correlation between disclinations and extrusion events is also related to the mechanical stress localization at the fivefold disclinations: The occurrence of disclinations in a flat surface produces local stress concentration (Irvine et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: It is energetically favorable to bend a flat surface, rather than to compress or to stretch it.
source: Generally, it is energetically favorable to bend a flat surface, rather than to compress or to stretch it (Landau et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: Local stress concentration can lead to a fivefold (positive Gaussian curvature) or a sevenfold (negative Gaussian curvature) disclination.
source: Thus, the local stress concentration can lead to a fivefold (positive Gaussian curvature) or a sevenfold (negative Gaussian curvature) disclination (Seung and Nelson, 1988; Guitter and Kardar, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Given a rigid substrate, fivefold disclinations are much more likely to provide relief for the high local stress concentration.
source: In our set-up and given that we consider a rigid substrate, fivefold disclinations are much more likely to provide relief for the high local stress concentration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation setup and theoretical understanding.

claim: High, out-of-plane, shear stress concentration is observed at extrusion sites.
source: We observe a high, out-of-plane, shear stress concentration (Figure 4b) as well as tensile and compressive stress pathways (Figure 4a) reminiscent of force chains in granular systems (Majmudar and Behringer, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by stress field data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Tensile and compressive stress pathways reminiscent of force chains in granular systems are observed.
source: We observe a high, out-of-plane, shear stress concentration (Figure 4b) as well as tensile and compressive stress pathways (Figure 4a) reminiscent of force chains in granular systems (Majmudar and Behringer, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by stress field data shown in Figure 4a and comparison with previous work on granular systems.

claim: The shear stress prior to extrusion exhibits oscillations with large magnitudes relative to the mean field, a stark departure from non-extruding counterparts.
source: The shear stress prior to extrusion exhibits oscillations with large magnitudes relative to the mean field, a stark departure from their non-extruding counterparts (see Appendix 1—figure 4 in Appendix 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by stress field data shown in Figure 4d and Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: Cells collectively migrate along the orientation of the minimal in-plane intercellular shear stress (plithotaxis).
source: Interestingly, the association of cell extrusion events with regions of high out-of-plane shear stress has parallels with the phenomenon of plithotaxis, where it was shown that cells collectively migrate along the orientation of the minimal in-plane intercellular shear stress (Tambe et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: High shear stress concentration hinders collective cell migration with cell extrusion providing a mechanism to re-establish the status quo.
source: In this context, based on the association of cell extrusion events with regions of high out-of-plane shear stress, we conjecture that high shear stress concentration hinders collective cell migration with cell extrusion providing a mechanism to re-establish the status quo.
evidence: This is a conjecture based on the simulation data and comparison with plithotaxis.

claim: There is an asymmetry in the intensity of stress in the compressive region at the head of the comet as opposed to the tensile region at the tail (≈5× higher).
source: Interestingly, there is an asymmetry in the intensity of stress in the compressive region at the head of the comet as opposed to the tensile region at the tail (≈5× higher).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of stress field data.

claim: For a single disclination, the energy is higher for a sevenfold disclination than a fivefold disclination.
source: Furthermore, for a single disclination, this energy is higher for a sevenfold disclination (Deem and Nelson, 1996) and in our case the rigid substrate defies any attempts by a sevenfold disclination to buckle and form a negative Gaussian curvature.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous theoretical work.

claim: The rigid substrate defies any attempts by a sevenfold disclination to buckle and form a negative Gaussian curvature.
source: Furthermore, for a single disclination, this energy is higher for a sevenfold disclination (Deem and Nelson, 1996) and in our case the rigid substrate defies any attempts by a sevenfold disclination to buckle and form a negative Gaussian curvature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation setup.

claim: The framework allows for cell–substrate and cell–cell adhesion forces to be tuned independently.
source: Our study presents a three-dimensional model of the collective migration-mediated cell elimination. Importantly, this framework allows for cell–substrate and cell–cell adhesion forces to be tuned independently.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling framework capabilities.

claim: Varying the relative strength of cell–cell and cell–substrate adhesion can allow cells to switch between distinct mechanical pathways to eliminate unwanted cells.
source: Our findings indeed suggest that varying the relative strength of cell–cell and cell–substrate adhesion can allow cells to switch between distinct mechanical pathways – leveraging defects in nematic and hexatic phases – to eliminate unwanted cells through: (i) cell extrusion at ±1/2 topological defects in the cell orientation field, consistent with experimental observations (Saw et al., 2017); and (ii) cell extrusion at fivefold disclinations in cell arrangement, where our results show a direct role of these disclinations in extruding the cells.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the simulation data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Increasing relative cell–cell adhesion increases the probability of an extruded cell being a fivefold disclination while weakening the correlation with +1/2 topological defects.
source: Focusing on the extruded cells, the results demonstrate that increasing relative cell–cell adhesion increases the probability of an extruded cell being a fivefold disclination while weakening the correlation with +1/2 topological defects.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the simulation data presented.

claim: The presented framework provides access to the local stress field, including the out-of-plane shear components.
source: Additionally, the presented framework provides access to the local stress field, including the out-of-plane shear components.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling framework capabilities demonstrated by the stress field data.

claim: In simulations with high extrusion events, confluency may be lost.
source: In this study, we intentionally narrowed our focus to the interplay of cell–cell and cell–substrate adhesion, without accounting for cell proliferation. In its absence, simulations with high extrusion events may lose confluency.
evidence: This is an observation about the simulation behavior.

claim: The identified mechanical routes to extrusion prevail in cases with both high and low number of extrusions, where confluency is maintained.
source: However, the identified mechanical routes to extrusion prevail in cases with both high and low number of extrusions, where confluency is maintained.
evidence: This is a statement about the robustness of the findings across different simulation conditions.

claim: The polarization dynamics is based on contact inhibition of locomotion (CIL) by aligning the polarity of the cell to the direction of the total interaction force acting on the cell.
source: To complete the model, the dynamics of front-rear cell polarity is introduced based on contact inhibition of locomotion (CIL) (Abercrombie and Heaysman, 1954; Abercrombie, 1979) by aligning the polarity of the cell to the direction of the total interaction force acting on the cell (Smeets et al., 2016; Peyret et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach supported by citations.

claim: The simulation parameters are chosen within the range that was previously shown to reproduce defect flow fields in epithelial layers.
source: All results are reported in dimensionless units, introduced throughout the text, and the simulation parameters are chosen within the range that was previously shown to reproduce defect flow fields in epithelial layers (Balasubramaniam et al., 2021; see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a statement about parameter selection supported by citation to previous work.
